question: Is it okay to ask for things while praying?
summary: The contradiction targets importunity — persistent, repetitive petitioning in prayer. Matthew 6:7-8 directly condemns it, with Jesus telling the disciples not to babble like the Gentiles because the Father already knows what they need before they ask. Luke 11:5-13 (the friend at midnight) and Luke 18:1-8 (the persistent widow) run the opposite way, with Jesus explicitly teaching that persistence in asking is exactly what gets rewarded.

reconcile.connective: Commentators read Matthew's ban as targeting hollow, mechanical babbling, not the sustained, faith-filled persistence Luke's parables commend.

discrepancy.relabel_reason: After genuine effort, no real critic could be confirmed pressing this specific pairing (Matthew 6:7-8's ban on 'vain repetitions' vs. Luke 11:5-13/18:1-8's teaching on persistent asking). Skeptics Annotated Bible's own 'Contradictions About Prayer' topical index (skepticsannotatedbible.com/prayer/contra2_list.html, 4 entries: 'Do Christians know how to pray?', 'Should you pray for everyone?', 'Should Christians pray in public?', 'Will those who call on the Lord be delivered?') does not include this pairing, and its Luke 11:5-13 'contra' flag cross-references a different tension (Matt 7:7-11 on whether prayer is reliably answered, not repetition vs. persistence). Donald Morgan's Infidels.org list and Jim Meritt's 1992 list likewise do not raise it. evilbible.com's 'Importunity in prayer commanded/condemned' framing (the source of this row) traces to an uncredited web compiler, not a named, on-topic critic. Every gathered PD commentator (Gill, JFB, Clarke, Henry) treats the two teachings as a routine and easy distinction (repetitive style vs. persistent substance), which together with the absence of an identifiable critic suggests 'probable_contradiction' may overstate this row.

pd_work.note: Henry treats this passage directly, distinguishing the 'vain repetitions'/'much speaking' Matthew 6:7 condemns from praying always: 'it is not much praying that is condemned; no, we are bid to pray always, but much speaking.'

excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Directly distinguishes the 'vain repetitions' Matt 6:7 condemns from persistent/repeated prayer, harmonizing it with Luke's importunity teaching (11:5-13, 18:1-8).
excerpts.source_note_text:
But when ye pray, use not vain repetitions--"Babble not" would be a better rendering, both for the form of the word--which in both languages is intended to imitate the sound--and for the sense, which expresses not so much the repetition of the same words as a senseless multiplication of them; as appears from what follows.
as the heathen do: for they think that they shall be heard for their much speaking--This method of heathen devotion is still observed by Hindu and Mohammedan devotees. With the Jews, says LIGHTFOOT, it was a maxim, that "Every one who multiplies prayer is heard." In the Church of Rome, not only is it carried to a shameless extent, but, as THOLUCK justly observes, the very prayer which our Lord gave as an antidote to vain repetitions is the most abused to this superstitious end; the number of times it is repeated counting for so much more merit. Is not this just that characteristic feature of heathen devotion which our Lord here condemns? But praying much, and using at times the same words, is not here condemned, and has the example of our Lord Himself in its favor.
